title: HSC 25 Trains on TERF Tactical Landings
description: 170821-N-XK809-002 SASEBO, Japan (Aug. 21, 2017) Pilots and crewmen assigned to Helicopter Sea Combat Squadron (HSC) 25 train on Terrain Flight (TERF) tactical landings during Talisman Saber 17 while embarked on the amphibious assault ship USS Bonhomme Richard (LHD 6). (U.S. Navy video by Mass Communication Specialist 3rd Class William Sykes/Released)
keywords: USS Bonhomme Richard (LHD 6), (HSC) 25, TERF, tactical landings

transcript.text: (guitar music)
^- Daniel James Treiber, Lieutenant
^in United States Navy.
^We're at the HT25 which is based in Guam.
I fly the MH-60 Sierra.
We have a pretty cool mission set.
All adverse, all across the board.
We're here stationed on the BHR for Detachment 6.
I've been flying for the Navy
just over four years now.
I've been flying with HSC25 for two years.
(soft music)
TERF is terrain flight and we practice it
for our overland mission set,
which includes personnel recovery,
overland SAR, or assault support.
So we practiced three yesterday,
one was called the tactical no-hover landing.
It's a lot more dynamic approach
where you come in fast.
Compare that to the DVE landings.
DVE's short for degraded visual environment.
We practiced a DVE steep and a DVE hover.
The DVE steep landing is used for moderate,
brown-out, or white-out.
And the DVE hover landing is used
for heavy brown-out or white-out situations.
Fun note about the DVE hover is
you actually split the controls,
so both pilots are manipulating
their controls all the way down to the deck.
I was on the cyclic, my co-pilot was on
the collective and I also had the pedals.
So he sets the descent rate
and I'm honoring our drift to make sure
we come straight down into the landing.
So it gets to a point where
if there's heavy dirt, and you can't see outside,
you can fly on the instruments
all the way down to the deck and land safely.
It was a nice respite from ship-ops too,
because we've been flying
to and from the ship all flow,
this is the first time for me
on this boat to go fly over land.
So you get to dust off the cobwebs
and get to fly low, low to the ground,
and practice the other mission sets
we haven't been able to so far in the flow.
So it's a lot more dynamic overland,
a lot more going on,
so you're more task-saturated flying over the land,
because there's a lot more things
that can come out and get ya.
Daytime, it's a lot more safe because obviously,
you have better visuals, you can see
the trees, you can see the changing terrain.
But at night when you're in goggles, NBDs,
it's harder and those things can surprise you
if you haven't done a good enough study
of the place where you're flying.
So, takes a lot more chart study
of where you're flying
to know where the hazards are,
and you have to be cognizant
your whole flight,
make sure you don't fly into it.
We follow the terrain on a chart
whenever we're flying over land,
to make sure we know where we on a chart
and a mountain doesn't come out and bite us.
(soft music)
It's a lot more control landing on a ship,
vise out over the land.
For instance, we have to do
a sweep-check over the land,
we fly it low and slow over the landing zone,
take a good look at it to make sure it's safe.
So we make sure that's safe,
we make sure we have a good egress point
for us to wave-off if necessary,
and then we'll come around again
and do it a lot more controlled.
Things you're looking for
is suitability to the zone,
the slope of the zone, our exit points, etc.
There's a lot more to consider,
whereas a ship, that's all taken care of for you.
You have the tower makin proper winds for you.
Whereas you have to find
the buffer winds over land.
